blocks.text: A college prototype connecting fingerprint verification, local blockchain payments, and simulated cash dispensing.
Submission draft • Software simulator demonstrated successfully. Physical assembly, firmware compilation/upload, and hardware acceptance remain pending.
This report describes an educational prototype. All currency is local test ETH or simulated rupees. No real cash or banking integration is involved.
Abstract

DecentraPay demonstrates how a wallet-approved blockchain transaction can trigger an observable hardware action. A browser interface guides the user through wallet connection, fingerprint verification, payment approval, and simulated cash dispensing. A Solidity smart contract on a local Ethereum-compatible blockchain receives test ETH and records a withdrawal request. A Node.js bridge verifies that request before commanding an ESP32 over USB.

The intended physical setup uses an R307 fingerprint sensor, an SG90 positional servo, and an LED. The sensor stores fingerprint templates locally. The servo moves a light flap to represent cash dispensing; the project does not feed or count banknotes. A clearly labelled hardware simulator permits software testing before assembly. The student's saved simulator journal contains three completed withdrawals and two rejected scan cases. Seventeen automated software tests pass. Physical results are deliberately recorded as pending.
Report map
Keywords: Web3, local Ethereum, smart contract, MetaMask, ESP32, fingerprint verification, serial communication, ATM prototype.
Educational problem

A blockchain payment is usually observed as a wallet balance or transaction record. An embedded-systems demonstration is usually observed as a sensor reading or motor movement. This project connects those two experiences in a small system that a student can operate and explain during a college evaluation. Its purpose is learning and demonstration, rather than replacing a bank or proposing a production cash network.
Objectives

items: Connect an enrolled demo wallet and verify the user's finger before authorizing a withdrawal session.
Execute a real local-chain transaction and show its hash, amount, and confirmation.
Allow one servo/LED cycle only after the bridge verifies a matching confirmed payment.
Handle common demonstration failures clearly, including unknown fingers, rejected wallet approval, and USB interruption.

blocks.text: Division of responsibilities

MetaMask controls the payment signature. The Solidity contract receives test ETH and emits a CashRequested event. The Node bridge maps a matching sensor slot to the demo wallet, verifies the transaction's sender, value, request ID and event, and sends the hardware command. The ESP32 communicates with the fingerprint sensor and controls the servo and LED. It does not run an Ethereum node.
Trust boundary

The contract cannot directly inspect a fingerprint, USB cable, servo shaft, or banknote. Those observations belong to the local bridge and device. The prototype therefore demonstrates Web3 execution with a trusted hardware connection. Its local development chain is a single node; describing the complete physical system as fully decentralized or trustless would be inaccurate.

The browser and bridge use local HTTP endpoints. The bridge and ESP32 exchange newline-delimited JSON over USB serial. All application assets are served locally after installation, so the normal demo does not require a public RPC service or testnet faucet.

The selected components are common educational modules. Purchase the target variants with labelled connectors and included cables; confirm actual specifications on arrival. Use soldered board headers and a breadboard arrangement that leaves the ESP32 GPIO connections accessible.

blocks.text: Why these parts

The R307 performs fingerprint capture, template storage, and matching internally. The ESP32 only needs the result and template slot. A positional servo provides an easily observed movement with a small amount of firmware. The LED indicates the movement interval. USB keeps the connection simple and avoids Wi-Fi configuration during the presentation.
Do not substitute a continuous-rotation servo for the 180-degree positional model. Do not assume that every R307 cable uses identical wire colors or connector orientation.
Supplier model links are included in docs/PRESENTATION_CHECKLIST.md. Prices and availability are intentionally not fixed in the report.

Wire with power disconnected. The GPIO assignments below are implemented in the current firmware and target the classic ESP32-WROOM-32 board. Verify the purchased R307 connector using its supplied pin diagram, not a generic photograph. The UART output must be compatible with ESP32 3.3 V logic.

rows: External rated supply; 5 V only if confirmed for this module
Join to ESP32 and peripheral grounds

blocks.text: Separate power, shared reference

The ESP32 receives board power through laptop USB. The servo receives power from the regulated external supply. Their grounds are connected so the control signal has a shared reference. Do not connect the external +5 V to the USB-powered board's 5 V or 3V3 pin. Do not power a servo from a GPIO or the board's 3V3 output. The board should use one power input. See the Espressif board guide [1].

The planned sensor is compatible with a 3.3 V microcontroller interface. If the supplied module instead has 5 V UART output, add a suitable UART level shifter before connecting its TX signal to the ESP32. Supply voltage and signal voltage are distinct specifications.
Start with the unloaded servo arm. Enclosure mounting follows a successful bench test. Leave access to the wiring and keep the arm clear of loose cables.

blocks.text: The browser displays the connected wallet, available test ETH, withdrawal amounts, verification stages, device connection state, and recent requests. It asks MetaMask to sign the payment and submits the resulting transaction hash to the bridge. Browser-reported success alone does not authorize dispensing; the bridge checks the chain independently.
Local interfaces

There is no browser endpoint that moves the servo directly. One request is active at a time, and the bridge records a dispense attempt before sending it. A process lock prevents two bridge/enrollment processes from owning the hardware journal simultaneously. Physical mode never silently falls back to simulated success.

Hardhat 2 was selected because the pinned packages were available offline in the implementation environment. The project uses the installed compiler package, rather than downloading a compiler during each demonstration.

DemoATM.sol contains one payable action: requestCash(bytes32 requestId). The user transfers local test ETH into the contract. The contract checks that the request ID is nonzero and unused, accepts only the supported values, marks the ID used, and emits a CashRequested event containing the request ID, customer address, payment in wei, and simulated rupee amount.

These are artificial demonstration rates. The wallet balance decreases by the payment plus gas. No rupees move through a bank, and no live price oracle is queried. Test ETH remains in the contract. The prototype has no automatic refund or contract-to-wallet withdrawal feature; a fresh demonstration can use an explicit local-chain reset.
Bridge checks before movement

items: The active fingerprint session is linked to the transaction's wallet and selected amount.
The chain ID, Hardhat instance, target contract, function call, and request ID match the current deployment.
The receipt is successful and includes the expected CashRequested event with the correct values.
The request has not already caused a dispensing attempt.

blocks.text: The contract prevents reusing a payment request ID. The bridge journal separately prevents repeating the physical command. These are different checks.

A direct payment to the contract without an authorized fingerprint session does not authorize physical dispensing. The contract itself has no fingerprint knowledge; the trusted bridge enforces that part of the workflow.

The existing Arduino sketch uses Adafruit Fingerprint Sensor Library, ESP32Servo, ArduinoJson 7, and the ESP32 Preferences API. USB communication runs at 115200 baud. The sensor uses hardware UART at 57600 baud on GPIO16/17. Arduino-ESP32 board support is installed through Boards Manager [2]; the library references are listed in [3–5].

blocks.text: The sensor retains its fingerprint template. The laptop records only the mapping between template slot 1 and the demo wallet. Simulator enrollment and serial-hardware enrollment use separate files, so a fake scan cannot fulfill physical-mode enrollment. Re-enrollment replaces slot 1.
Dispensing sequence

The default servo movement is 30 degrees to 100 degrees and back to 30 degrees. The firmware holds the dispense position for one second, then returns and turns off the LED. It stores the most recent request ID before movement to refuse immediate repeated dispensing, including after reboot. The full request history is protected by the laptop journal.

An acknowledgement means the firmware finished its command sequence. It is not a measurement of shaft position or cash output. There is no cash sensor. USB opening can reset the board and return the servo to its resting position.

Verification status: firmware exists, but Arduino compilation/upload and all real sensor/servo observations are pending. The required board toolchain and physical components were unavailable during document preparation.

blocks.text: Failures do not imply refunds

An unknown finger is rejected before wallet payment. Rejecting the MetaMask prompt does not send a dispensing command. A pending payment waits for confirmation. A mismatched or reverted transaction does not dispense. A lost USB acknowledgement after payment produces an uncertain result rather than an automatic retry. A confirmed payment remains on-chain even if the motor cannot be observed.
Restart and reset

Restarting only the bridge preserves the running chain and journal. Interrupted payments or dispensing are marked uncertain, and stale fingerprint sessions are cancelled. The explicit demo:reset command starts a fresh local demonstration and archives old records. Enrollment is retained. The user may need to clear stale MetaMask activity after restarting the chain.

The browser remembers an outstanding transaction hash so it can check the same payment instead of asking for another. A unique deployment ID prevents a reset from treating an old payment as current, even when the new contract has the same address.

Evidence captured 26 October 2026. The student confirmed that MetaMask withdrawals work. The saved local journal contains three completed simulator payments. None is a physical hardware acceptance result.
Automated verification

All 17 automated tests pass on an isolated in-process Hardhat EVM. Coverage includes supported and invalid amounts, event/value correctness, three authenticated withdrawals, wrong wallet/fingerprint, session cancellation/expiry, unrelated payments, pending and reverted transactions, duplicate prevention, lost acknowledgements, restart behavior, changed-chain detection, simulator boundaries, HTTP origin checks, and process locking.

The web build and Solidity compilation also pass. The saved test and build logs are included with this report. The journal also records an unrecognized-fingerprint case and a simulated sensor-communication error. These exercise software behavior; they do not establish the real sensor's accuracy or hardware reliability.

The evidence is a snapshot of local files. A reset can remove the corresponding chain from memory, and these hashes have no public explorer link. Exact hashes and the deployment identifier are preserved in presentation/evidence/demo-snapshot.json.

blocks.caption: Figure 2. Actual student-provided screenshot before correction: the local network is connected, but the selected wallet has zero test ETH and is not linked to the enrolled fingerprint.

blocks.text: Diagnosis

The screenshot shows the selected wallet beginning 0xA84263, while the configured simulator enrollment maps slot 1 to 0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8. Connecting to the correct network is necessary, but it does not select or fund the expected account. The app correctly rejected the unlinked wallet.
Resolution and subsequent result

The student imported the supplied public local-development account into MetaMask, selected DecentraPay Local, and reconnected that account on the ATM page. The student then confirmed that withdrawals worked. The completed simulator journal entries on the preceding page provide separate software-run evidence; this screenshot itself shows the earlier failure, not a successful withdrawal.
Presentation preparation: add a screenshot of a successful withdrawal and actual assembly photographs after physical testing. Do not relabel this troubleshooting image as a hardware demonstration.

blocks.text: Use the laptop as the screen. Mount the fingerprint sensor on the front, the LED above the flap, and the servo inside on an insulating base. Keep the rear removable, the cable accessible, and the arm clear of wires. Printed labels should identify fingerprint verification and simulated cash dispensing. A real-note feeding mechanism is unnecessary.

Photograph the assembled hardware and record a short real demonstration as an explicitly labelled backup. Replace pending statements only after those observations exist.
The final acceptance target is three consecutive physical withdrawals, not three simulator results. Install all tools before the venue visit and rehearse on the exact laptop while offline.

DecentraPay implements a small, explainable link between fingerprint authorization, a wallet-signed smart-contract payment, and device control. The local software demonstration is working and has supporting journal entries and automated tests. The remaining implementation milestone is purchasing, assembling, compiling/uploading, and verifying the physical hardware.

The design deliberately limits its claims: one local node, a trusted laptop bridge, artificial rupee values, and servo movement instead of actual cash handling. It does not establish production security, public-network decentralization, financial settlement, or guaranteed physical delivery. For the college project, completion means a clear explanation and repeatable observed hardware demonstrations within those boundaries.
